questions.q: In the Fairmont Logistics case study, what happens during the reconnaissance stage?
options: An employee opens a malicious email attachment
A backdoor beacons out to a command-and-control server
An attacker runs an internet-wide scan that finds Fairmont's exposed ports
An attacker exfiltrates customer data out of the network
questions.explain: Reconnaissance is the first stage — the attacker scans for exposed services before ever contacting an employee.

questions.q: What real control is named as a defense against the weaponization and delivery stage (the phishing email)?
options: Encrypting data at rest and in transit
A compliance framework governing breach notification
A firewall egress rule blocking outbound C2 traffic
Email filtering and security-awareness training that helps an employee question an unexpected attachment
questions.explain: Delivery is stopped before the fact by filtering and by training employees to recognize and question suspicious attachments.

questions.q: Why does least-privilege access (role-based authorization) matter at the exploitation stage, even after a malicious macro successfully runs?
options: It limits the compromised account's access, containing the damage the macro can actually cause
It automatically deletes the malicious file from the system
It has no real effect once exploitation has already occurred
It completely prevents the macro from ever executing in the first place
questions.explain: Least privilege doesn't stop exploitation itself, but it limits what the attacker can do with the access they gained.

questions.q: What pattern, taught in the Wireshark lesson, shows up again during the command-and-control (C2) stage of this case study?
options: A host beaconing out to the same unfamiliar destination on a steady interval
A single DNS query followed immediately by its response
A port scan hitting many destination ports at once
A clean three-way handshake completing normally
questions.explain: C2 beaconing produces a regular, unfamiliar outbound pattern — the same kind of signal Lesson 30 taught you to notice.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why does stopping an attack earlier in the kill chain matter so much?
options: The kill chain stages always happen in a random, unpredictable order
Each stage that succeeds makes the next one easier, and the eventual cost of cleanup, legal exposure, and notification rises sharply
Only the final stage of an attack ever causes any real damage
Early stages of an attack are technically impossible to detect with any control
questions.explain: Blocking reconnaissance costs a firewall rule; cleaning up after exfiltration costs a forensic investigation and regulatory exposure.
